extracted.intended_audience: neuroscience researchers and clinicians studying narcolepsy, emotion, and fMRI methods
extracted.subtask_description: Design, acquisition, and analysis protocol for an EEG–video–fMRI experiment that elicits and maps neural correlates of laughter and emotion-induced cataplexy in drug‑naive children/adolescents with narcolepsy type 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant inclusion criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients were proposed to participate if the following inclusion criteria were satisfied: (1) drug‑naive children from 8 to 16 years old with NT1, (2) a diagnosis of NT1 according to the current criteria (American Academy of Sleep Medicine, 2014), (3) proven CSF hypocretin‑1 deficiency, (4) cataplexy onset for no more than 2 years, and (5) video documentation of cataplectic attacks during a standardized video session no longer than 6 months before the neuroimaging experimental sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strict, pre-specified clinical and laboratory inclusion criteria (age range, diagnostic criteria, biochemical confirmation, recent onset, recent video documentation) to select homogeneous, drug‑naive participants representative of genuine emotion‑induced cataplexy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient-specific stimulus selection to maximize cataplexy
rubrics_metrics.description: To maximize the chance of recording cataplexy in the MRI scanner, adopt a patient‑specific protocol by selecting the funny videos that were previously successful in the standardized video session. Videos were digitally recorded and edited to remove commercials. The resulting videos were 8 min and 30 s in length. Two to three videos were presented to each patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor humorous stimuli to each subject's preferences based on prior standardized sessions; remove extraneous content (commercials); present multiple runs to increase probability of eliciting events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral instructions during scanning
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients were scanned while passively viewing an entire video without any specific task requirement. They were told they should try to keep their head fixed, but they could smile or even laugh if the comic was funny, and that they did not have to suppress emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage natural emotional reactions but request minimization of head motion. Do not force an active task—use passive viewing to elicit spontaneous laughter/cataplexy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video run structure and baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Each fMRI run was organized in 30 s of baseline during which the patient was instructed to watch a white cross on a black screen followed by one funny video. Each video was 8 min and 30 s and the relative fMRI scan time was 510 s. Two to three fMRI runs were repeated in each session for every patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a short, well‑defined baseline block preceding long naturalistic stimulus blocks; repeat runs to increase sampling of rare events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑scan subjective humor rating
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the scan, each subject was asked to rate each cartoon for humor intensity (i.e., degree of funniness) on a scale of 1 to 10, with 1 and 10 as the least and most funny, respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect per‑run subjective funniness ratings to relate neural responses to subjective enjoyment; use a simple anchored numeric scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygraphic multimodal recording during fMRI
rubrics_metrics.description: fMRI data were acquired synchronously with EEG, mylohyoid muscle activity (subchin EMG), ECG, and the video of the patient's face (small camcorder positioned on the head coil).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simultaneous EEG, EMG, ECG, and video to identify behavioral/physiologic correlates (laughter, swallowing, cataplexy) and to improve timing and artifact modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: EMG acquisition and filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface EMG activity was recorded from the mylohyoid muscle. EMG activity from the mylohyoid muscle was filtered between 50 and 500 Hz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record submental/mylohyoid EMG to detect bursts during laughter and transient losses of tone during cataplexy; apply bandpass filtering (50–500 Hz) appropriate for muscle activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video‑polygraphic documentation for event timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The simultaneously recorded video during scanning allowed patients to be checked for physiological facial movements, laughter, and the appearance of cataplexy. For the purpose of the work, chin EMG and video recordings were essential for recognizing the exact time and duration of each cataplectic event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on synchronized video + EMG to establish precise onsets/offsets of behavioral events; retain video for offline verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert consensus definition of cataplexy events
rubrics_metrics.description: Three sleep medicine experts reviewed the cataplexy video recordings and identified the main facial features and the polygraphic picture of cataplectic attacks. They subsequently reviewed the video‑polygraphic recordings obtained during fMRI independently to identify onsets/offsets of laughter/smiles and cataplectic 'negative motor' phenomena. 'Cataplectic attacks' were considered only the events for which the judgments of the raters were concordant. In case of disagreement, the clinical features of cataplectic attacks of that patient, as recorded in the sleep laboratory, were reviewed and compared with the events recorded in the scan; only when a consensus was reached was the event considered a 'cataplectic event' to minimize false positives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple blinded expert raters and require concordance; resolve disagreements by reference to prior clinical footage for that patient to reduce false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding false positives via lab comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of disagreement among raters about an event, the clinical features of cataplectic attacks of that patient, as recorded in the sleep laboratory, were reviewed and compared with the events recorded in the scan; only when a consensus was reached was the event considered a 'cataplectic event' to minimize the risk of false‑positive events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare candidate in‑scanner events with previously documented lab attacks for the same subject to validate ambiguous episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: EEG preprocessing and artifact suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: After off‑line correction of the gradient artifacts and filtering of the EEG signal, the EEG data were reviewed and preprocessed according to published methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply MRI gradient artifact removal and appropriate EEG preprocessing pipelines before inspection; reference established methods (e.g., cited papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: fMRI acquisition parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional data were acquired using a Philips Intera system at 3 T and a gradient‑echo EPI sequence from 30 axial contiguous slices (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 35 ms, in‑plane matrix = 80 × 80, voxel size = 3 × 3 × 3 mm) over two to three 8 min 30 s runs (255 volumes per run) with continuous simultaneous video‑polygraphic recording. A high‑resolution T1‑weighted anatomic image was acquired for anatomical reference and volumetric analysis (170 sagittal slices, TR = 9.9 ms, TE = 4.6 ms, voxel size = 1 × 1 × 1 mm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report full scanner and sequence parameters so results are reproducible; include high‑res anatomy for registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: fMRI preprocessing pipeline
rubrics_metrics.description: All functional volumes were slice‑time corrected, realigned to the first volume acquired, normalized to the MNI template, and smoothed with 8 × 8 × 8 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard SPM preprocessing (slice timing, motion realignment, spatial normalization, smoothing) with an explicit smoothing kernel reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion confound modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The GLM included confounds represented by 24 realignment parameters (six scan realignment parameters from image preprocessing and a Volterra expansion of these). To further assess influence of head motion, head motion was quantified by computing vector distances (derived from the x, y, and z translational realignment corrections) between sequential functional volumes; vector distances per time point were assigned to 'laughter', 'cataplexy', and 'baseline' and submitted to one‑way ANOVA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model motion using expanded realignment regressors and explicitly test whether motion differs across conditions by computing frame‑to‑frame displacement vectors and statistical comparison across conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling effects of interest in the GLM
rubrics_metrics.description: For each EPI session one GLM was constructed including (1) the effects of interest (laughter and/or cataplexy), represented as blocks (with duration defined by the video) convolved with canonical hemodynamic response function; (2) the confounds, represented by 24 realignment parameters; and (3) the video‑based physiologic facial movements (i.e., swallowing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model events/epochs with durations defined from video/EMG and convolve with canonical HRF; include both motion regressors and video‑derived physiological regressors to reduce physiological/artifact contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of video‑based physiologic regressors
rubrics_metrics.description: Video‑based physiologic facial movements (e.g., swallowing) were included as confounds in the GLM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use video annotations to model facial/physiological movements that could confound BOLD signal—include them as regressors of no interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical contrast and random‑effects group analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical parametric maps were generated from linear contrasts between conditions in each participant (laughter > baseline; cataplexy > baseline; cataplexy > laughter). The contrast images from each subject were then submitted to a second‑level group analysis using the random‑effect approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute first‑level contrasts per subject, then perform second‑level random‑effects analyses to infer population effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical thresholding rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The threshold for statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 corrected for false discovery rate (FDR) or p < 0.001 uncorrected if the BOLD maps did not reveal any change at the more conservative threshold. In these uncorrected maps, an extent threshold of five contiguous voxels was applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefine conservative multiple‑comparison correction (FDR p<0.05). If necessary, allow less conservative uncorrected thresholds (p<0.001) but apply an explicit voxel extent threshold and report both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single‑subject support for group findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Single‑subject analyses supported group findings: amygdala and insula positive BOLD changes were detected in 8 of 10 patients, anterior cingulate/VMPFC increments in 9 of 10, brainstem changes in 6 of 10 at p < 0.05 FDR (observed in every patient at p < 0.001 uncorrected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report single‑subject prevalence to substantiate group‑level effects and indicate robustness across participants; include thresholding used for single‑subject inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole‑brain correlation analyses with clinical/behavioral variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform whole‑brain second‑level correlation analyses to test for linear relations between BOLD signal changes and main clinical measurements, including age at disease onset, duration of disease, cataplexy frequency, ESS score, mean sleep latency, number of SOREMPs at the MSLT, number of observed smiles/laughter events during scanning, and postscanning ratings of the videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predefine clinical and behavioral covariates of interest and perform whole‑brain correlation analyses to assess whether neural responses relate to individual characteristics; report null results when no significant correlations are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Session timing and sleepiness control
rubrics_metrics.description: Data acquisition was performed in a dimly lit room during the afternoon. Patients were asked to take a brief nap before the recordings to reduce sleepiness and avoid its confounding effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control circadian and sleepiness confounds by scheduling sessions appropriately and allowing brief naps beforehand to reduce spontaneous sleep onset during scanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral quantification of cataplexy frequency and sleepiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cataplexy frequency was assessed and subjective sleepiness was quantified by a modified version of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (mESS). Before the fMRI scan sessions, the ESS score and the frequency of cataplexy were assessed in each patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect standardized behavioral/clinical measures (cataplexy frequency, ESS) prior to scanning to characterize participants and enable correlation analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of head motion — reporting and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: No subject was excluded from subsequent analysis for excessive head motion. To assess whether movement affected one condition more than others, vector distances were computed and compared across conditions (no differences in head motion were recorded among cataplexy (0.45 ± 0.29 mm), laughter (0.42 ± 0.20 mm), and baseline vision (0.40 ± 0.25 mm; F(2,22) = 0.06, p > 0.8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report motion statistics per condition and justify inclusion/exclusion decisions; if no condition‑specific motion differences are found, inclusion without exclusion can be justified, but motion must still be modeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event coding as blocks with video‑defined durations
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and cataplexy events were represented as blocks (with duration defined by the video) convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function for GLM analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use video/EMG‑derived event durations to define block regressors rather than treating all events as instantaneous; convolve with HRF to model expected BOLD response.
